column2: Fatḥ al-Qawī al-Matīn (The Opening from the All-Strong, the Firm): A Commentary on the Forty and the Completion of the Fifty by al-Nawawī and Ibn Rajab, may Allah have mercy on them both
By ʿAbd al-Muḥsin ibn Ḥamad al-ʿAbbād al-Badr
In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

All praise is due to Allah, the Bestower of abundant gifts and the Giver of ample blessings. I bear witness that none has the right to be worshipped except Allah alone, without partner, the Possessor of grace, kindness, generosity and munificence; and I bear witness that Muḥammad is His servant and Messenger, the master of the Arabs and the non-Arabs, singled out by his Lord with concise, comprehensive speech (jawāmiʿ al-kalim).

O Allah, send prayers, peace and blessings upon him and upon his family, people of noble deeds and fine qualities; upon his Companions, lamps in the darkness of night, whom Allah honoured by making them the best of a nation that is itself the best of nations; and upon all who came after them following in their footsteps, their hearts free of rancour towards the believers and sound.

To proceed: among the subjects on which scholars have written concerning the hadiths of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ are “forties”, that is, collections of forty of the hadiths of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

This is because of a hadith reported on the virtue of memorising forty of the hadiths of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. In the introduction to his Forty, al-Nawawī mentioned that it is reported from nine of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, whom he named,
and he said, “The hadith masters agree that it is a weak hadith, even though its routes are many.” He mentioned that in compiling the Forty he did not rely on it, but on other hadiths,

such as his words ﷺ, “Let the one who is present among you convey to the one who is absent,” and his words, “May Allah make radiant a person who heard my words and retained them…” to the end of the hadith. He named thirteen scholars who compiled forties,

the first of them ʿAbdullāh ibn al-Mubārak and the last Abū Bakr al-Bayhaqī, and after listing them he said, “…and countless others among the earlier and later scholars.” He also said, “Some scholars compiled forty hadiths on the fundamentals of the religion,
some on its subsidiary rulings, some on jihād, some on zuhd, some on etiquette and some on sermons. All of these are righteous aims; may Allah the Exalted be pleased with those who pursued them.

I have considered it more important than all of this to compile forty hadiths that comprise all of that, each of them a great principle of the religion, of which the scholars have said that Islam revolves around it,
or that it is half of Islam, or a third of it, or the like. I have also committed myself to including only authentic hadiths in this Forty, most of them in the two Ṣaḥīḥs of al-Bukhārī and Muslim.

I mention them without their chains of narration so that they are easy to memorise and their benefit becomes widespread, if Allah wills… Everyone who desires the Hereafter should know these hadiths, because of the important matters they contain and the guidance they give to all acts of obedience; that is clear to whoever reflects on them.”

The hadiths that al-Nawawī (may Allah have mercy on him) collected are forty-two; they were called “the Forty” by rounding, dropping the extra fraction. This book of al-Nawawī, together with his book Riyāḍ al-Ṣāliḥīn, has been blessed with acceptance among people,

and both became famous and received much attention. The first book that comes to mind when directing beginners in hadith is this Forty of Imam al-Nawawī (may Allah have mercy on him). Ibn Rajab al-Ḥanbalī (may Allah have mercy on him) added to it eight hadiths of comprehensive speech (jawāmiʿ al-kalim),

completing the number at fifty, and he explained them in a book he named Jāmiʿ al-ʿUlūm wa-l-Ḥikam fī Sharḥ Khamsīn Ḥadīthan min Jawāmiʿ al-Kalim (The Compendium of Knowledge and Wisdom: A Commentary on Fifty Hadiths of Comprehensive Speech). Commentaries on Imam al-Nawawī's Forty are many, some brief and some lengthy,

and the most extensive of them is the commentary of Ibn Rajab al-Ḥanbalī (may Allah have mercy on him). I decided to explain this Forty, together with Ibn Rajab's addition, in a medium-length commentary close to concise, the explanation of each hadith consisting of several paragraphs

and closing with some of the lessons drawn from the hadith. In this commentary I have benefited from the commentaries of al-Nawawī, Ibn Daqīq al-ʿĪd, Ibn Rajab and Ibn ʿUthaymīn on the Forty, and from Fatḥ al-Bārī by Ibn Ḥajar al-ʿAsqalānī.

I have named it Fatḥ al-Qawī al-Matīn fī Sharḥ al-Arbaʿīn wa-Tatimmat al-Khamsīn li-l-Nawawī wa-Ibn Rajab (may Allah have mercy on them both). Al-Matīn (the Firm) is one of the names of Allah; Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says in Sūrat al-Dhāriyāt:

“Indeed, it is Allah who is the Provider, the Possessor of strength, the Firm” [al-Dhāriyāt 51:58]. It means the One of intense strength, as stated in the books of tafsīr. I urge students of knowledge to memorise these fifty hadiths, which are among the comprehensive words of the noble Messenger, upon him be the best of blessings and the most complete peace.

I ask Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, to make this commentary beneficial as He made its original beneficial; He is All-Hearing, Ever-Responsive. May Allah send prayers, peace and blessings upon His servant and Prophet Muḥammad, and upon all his family and Companions.
End of the commentary. All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds, and may Allah send prayers, peace and blessings upon His servant and Messenger Muḥammad, and upon his family and Companions.
